{{short description|British-French physicist and electrical engineer}}
{{distinguish|Owen Story|Robert Llewellyn}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Llewelyn Robert Owen Storey'''<ref name="storey1967">{{cite journal |last1=Storey |first1=Llewelyn Robert Owen |title=Preliminary results on VLF propagation in the lower magnetosphere obtained by the FR 1 satellite |journal=Space Research |date=1967 |issue=7 |pages=588–603 |publisher=North Holland Publishing Co. |location=Amsterdam}}</ref> (born 5 November 1927; also known as '''L. R. O. Storey''',<ref name="NSSDC-VLF">{{cite web |title=FR 1:VLF Receiver |url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/experiment/display.action?id=1965-101A-01 |publisher=NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive |access-date=11 December 2020}}</ref> '''L. R. Owen Storey''',<ref name="ethw-storey">{{cite web |title=Owen Storey |url=https://ethw.org/Owen_Storey |publisher=Engineering and Technology History Wiki |access-date=11 December 2020 |date=29 January 2019}}</ref> and '''Owen Storey'''<ref name="ethw-storey"/>) is a British [[physicist]] and [[electrical engineering|electrical engineer]] who has worked and lived most of his adult life in [[France]]. He is known for his research on the [[atmosphere of Earth|Earth's atmosphere]], especially [[whistler (radio)|whistlers]]—[[very low frequency]] (VLF) radio waves caused by [[lightning]] strikes—and the [[magnetosphere]]. He was the first person to prove whistlers are caused by lightning strikes and to deduce the plasmasphere's existence. He was heavily involved in designing scientific instruments for [[FR-1 (satellite)|FR-1]], a 1965 French-American satellite, and subsequent studies and experiments using data FR-1 collected.

==Early life==
Storey was born on 5 November 1927 in [[Crowborough]], [[England]], [[United Kingdom]].<ref name="ethw-storey"/> He received a Bachelor of Arts degree in [[natural science]]s in 1948 and a PhD in [[physics]] in 1953, both from the [[University of Cambridge]].<ref name="ethw-storey"/> He became interested in [[whistler (radio)|whistlers]] during his time as a graduate student.<ref name="ethw-storey"/> In fact, Storey in his 1953 PhD [[thesis|dissertation]] was the first person to realize the propagation of VLF radio waves after lightning strikes causes whistlers.<ref name="ethw-storey"/><ref name="gallagher">{{cite web |last1=Gallagher |first1=D. L. |title=Discovering the Plasmasphere |url=https://plasmasphere.nasa.gov/discovery.html |website=Space Plasma Physics |publisher=NASA [[Marshall Space Flight Center]] |access-date=11 December 2020 |location=Huntsville, AL |date=27 May 2015}}</ref><ref name="RAH1965">{{cite book|title=Whistlers and Related Ionospheric Phenomena|author=[[Robert Helliwell|Robert A. Helliwell]]|publisher=[[Dover Publications|Dover Publications, Inc]]|year=2006|isbn=978-0-486-44572-4}} Originally published by Stanford University Press, Stanford, California (1965).</ref> Around the same time, Storey had posited the existence of whistlers meant [[plasma (physics)|plasma]] was present in Earth's atmosphere, and that it moved radio waves in the same direction as [[Earth's magnetic field]] lines.<ref name="ethw-storey"/><ref name="gallagher"/> From this he deduced but was unable to conclusively prove the existence of the [[plasmasphere]], a region of cold plasma extending from the upper [[ionosphere]] far into the [[magnetosphere]].<ref name="ethw-storey"/>

After obtaining his doctorate, Storey worked in England, and then [[Canada]] and the [[United States]], before becoming an employee of the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] (''Centre national de la recherche scientifique''; CNRS) in 1959.<ref name="ethw-storey"/>

==Career and research==
[[File:FR 1 assembly.jpg|thumb|FR-1 mounted on a [[Scout (rocket family)|Scout rocket]] prior to launch in 1965; from left to right, C. Fayard, X. Namy, J. P. Causse, and '''L. R. O. Storey''']]

===FR-1: whistlers and the plasmasphere===
{{Further|FR-1 (satellite)}}
In 1963 Storey became scientific director of the joint French-American [[FR-1 (satellite)|FR-1 satellite program]].<ref name="ethw-storey"/> He specified the satellite's scientific instruments, working in concert with Dr. Robert W. Rochelle and Sam Stevens of [[NASA]]'s [[Goddard Space Flight Center]] (GSFC).<ref name ="NSSDC">{{cite web|url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1965-101A|title=General information about FR-1|publisher=NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive|access-date=11 December 2020}}</ref>

FR-1 was launched on 6 December 1965.<ref name ="NSSDC"/> The mission objective was to study the composition and structure of the [[ionosphere]], [[plasmasphere]], and [[magnetosphere]] by measuring the propagation of VLF waves and the local [[electron density]] of [[plasma (physics)|plasma]] in those atmospheric layers.<ref name="aa1965">{{cite web|url=https://history.nasa.gov/AAchronologies/1965.pdf|title=Aeronautics and Astronautics, 1965|publisher=NASA|page=540|access-date=11 December 2020}}</ref><ref name="ducrocq">{{cite journal |last1=Ducrocq |first1=Albert |title=La course aux deux infinis |journal=[[Air & Cosmos]] |date=25 March 1963 |volume=1 |page=10 |language=fr |issn=1240-3113}}</ref> For the VLF wave experiments, stations located on land in [[Seine-Port]], France (at the [[Sainte-Assise transmitter]]), and [[Balboa, Panama|Balboa]], [[Panama]], transmitted signals at 16.8&nbsp;kHz and 24&nbsp;kHz, respectively, while the satellite's magnetic and electric sensors orbiting about {{convert|750|km}} away analyzed the magnetic field of the received wave.<ref name="NSSDC-VLF"/><ref name="aubry">{{cite journal |last1=Aubry |first1=M. P. |title=Some results of the FR-1 satellite experiment on the VLF wave field in the zone close to the transmitter |journal=Journal of Atmospheric and Terrestrial Physics |date=1968 |volume=30 |issue=6 |pages=1161–1182 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9169(68)80005-4|bibcode=1968JATP...30.1161A }}</ref>

Principal researchers who studied both the VLF and electron density data collected by FR-1 included Storey, as well as the French scientists Dr. M. P. Aubry of [[Centre national d'études des télécommunications|CNET]] and Dr. C. Renard.<ref name="NSSDC-VLF"/> Aubry published his results in 1968, while Storey published initial findings in 1967 before the mission's ultimate end.<ref name="NSSDC-VLF"/><ref name="aubry"/> Northern Irish physicist [[James Sayers (physicist)|James Sayers]]—an electron density expert—was also involved in the electron density experiments.<ref name="NSSDC-ED">{{cite web |title=FR 1:Electron Density |url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/experiment/display.action?id=1965-101A-02 |publisher=NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive |access-date=11 December 2020}}</ref>

Data collected by FR-1 helped prove the existence of the plasmasphere. Prior to their work on FR-1, both Aubry and Storey had studied whistlers. From earlier whistler research Storey deduced the existence of the plasmasphere but was unable to conclusively prove it. In 1963 American scientist [[Don Carpenter (electrical engineer)|Don Carpenter]] and Soviet [[astronomer]] [[Konstantin Gringauz]]—independently of each other, and the latter using data from the ''[[Luna 2]]'' spacecraft—experimentally proved the plasmasphere and [[plasmapause]]'s existence, building on Storey's thinking.<ref name="gallagher"/> Aubry and Storey's post-1965 studies of FR-1 VLF and electron density data further corroborated this: VLF waves in the ionosphere occasionally passed through a thin layer of plasma into the magnetosphere, [[normal (geometry)|normal]] to the direction of [[Earth's magnetic field]].<ref name="storey1967"/><ref name="aubry"/>{{rp|1181}}

===Later career===
After his work on FR-1, Storey headed his own research group which continued studying VLF waves using data gathered the satellite.<ref name="ethw-storey"/>  It transferred to a laboratory in [[Orléans]] from its original [[Paris]] location in the early 1970s.<ref name="ethw-storey"/> This group's research focused on developing methods for measuring the properties of space plasmas using [[dipole antenna]]s, and [[wave distribution function]] (WDF) analysis.<ref name="ethw-storey"/> For the plasma measurement research Storey and his group collaborated with [[West Germany|West German]] and [[Sweden|Swedish]] programs during the [[International Magnetospheric Study]] of 1976 to 1979, allowing them to carry out further experiments on [[rocket]]s.<ref name="ethw-storey"/>

In 1983 Storey joined the research faculty of [[Stanford University]]'s Electrical Engineering Department.<ref name="ethw-storey"/> From 1987 to 1989 he served as a senior visiting scientist at [[NASA Headquarters]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], and then as a WDF analysis software developer at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.<ref name="ethw-storey"/>

Storey retired in 1992.<ref name="ethw-storey"/> In 1997 he received the [[IEEE Heinrich Hertz Medal]] for his lifelong research on whistlers.<ref name="ethw-storey"/><ref name="ethw-hhm">{{cite web |title=IEEE Heinrich Hertz Medal |url=https://ethw.org/IEEE_Heinrich_Hertz_Medal |publisher=Engineering and Technology History Wiki |access-date=11 December 2020 |date=16 November 2016}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Storey is a member of the [[American Geophysical Union]].<ref name="ethw-storey"/> He and his wife live in [[southern France]]; they have three children together.<ref name="ethw-storey"/>
